- Feeling like I’ve lost vision?
- Is it possible to abstract and logic away your own vision via incessant self reflection and pruning?
- I have always always struggled with the feeling that I fundamentally don’t have vision
- Regardless of how well I am able to see other people’s vision, I fail to see the same in myself
- Every time I tell myself that the horizons have never been clearer because “I should just do whatever the hell I want”, I feel more boxed in than ever
- This is not necessarily a surprise; the weight of open spaces, and the command to “go run around”, inspires a particular kind of anxiety and dizziness and fear that leads one to prefer the enclosed
- I fear my creations will forever be confined to technical prowess and anatomical correctness and limits
- I find it so hard to work with free flowing narratives and uncertain paths forward
- Both technically, in that I am quite literally unsure how to do it, but more importantly mentally and emotionally. Not only do I feel like such a fledgling in any aspect of ability to create a story, but it (either alongside, because of, or causing that) is hard to get myself to even want to attempt to do so.
- I feel this particular aversion to trying, and I cannot tell whether that is simple beginners anxiety that I do not want to see how bad my first attempt will look, or whether it’s simply “not for me” and I am attempting to force my creative power into a place that is has no business existing within
- Which is really a hard thing for me to deal with; the thought of “what if I just don’t like doing it?”
- I have failed to get into animation, again and again, for a year now. The only finished works, or more correctly sketches, I have finished have been very small self contained studies of rope movement, bouncing ball physics, etc
- I cannot help but compare this to my foray into drawing, where thoughts of technical practice and ability came almost two years after my creating many strange, esoteric, “experimental” works for which I had no basis but my desire to make colors and shapes appear
- And even this too, I feel, has become so polluted recently by the awareness of perspective, and lighting, and form
- And I have not really yet known any time where this has ever been present with my relationship with animation; despite how badly I wish for the idea of me animating things, I nevertheless have not been able to progress my relationship with it for over a year past fitful stages of contextless technical practice, more concerned with whether I’m using the best animation software than with any of the things I am animating
- I cannot help but think that I am forcing myself into animation, which simultaneously seems at odds with myself and my desire so badly to produce animations, and forces my mind to think I am using “I don’t like animating” as an excuse to not do the hard work involved
- Which, in turn, forces me to think about what I even consider animating to be, and the reality that whatever shiny bright idea I have of visionary and polished animations being produced in hours is not real, neither for me nor anyone else, and that I simply don’t know what it’s like to animate yet
- And, circling back, the deep and fundamental doubt that I have ever had any vision at all, besides for small brief unsustained flashes
- Wondering how I cooked some of the shit I cooked in the past
- It almost feels like I had good feasible achievable ideas, and then I achieved them, and now I have none left. They did not replenish, like I figured they would have; they’re just gone now

- Noticing this trend where I have a vague and foggy idea of a general concept in my head, but the first time it is ever concretized is when I make a specific realization about a part of my life, and only then do I really fully grasp the abstract concept
- For example, two of my recent entries have been about the idea of messages not needing to be read for the content to nevertheless have meaning in the world
- That “idea” has existed in my head for a long time in many different forms - the general idea that the existence of things are not justified by their being viewed or experienced by a human being, because they are being experienced by “the world” at all times, which is no more or less important than a human
- But I really only put it to words in the context of my ideas of what this journal will be and who will ever read it, if anybody; I essentially came to the realization that it doesn’t matter who reads this because ultimately the importance this journal will have is not tied to who reads it and what they think about it, the importance of this journal exists within the simple fact that it exists, and I created it
- And “only then” was I later able to realize, “concretely”, the larger abstract concept of messages justifying their own existence
- The idea that there are so many people that, well, “at least one” would…

- All messages are read
- I’m not sure how to phrase this
- A message unsent is not a message unread
- Messages not read by the intended recipient are nevertheless read
- The intent, or meaning, of some sort of message is not only realized when it is received by a recipient, read, and has affected them whatever way it may (intended or unintended)
- Messages retain their full body of force from the moment they are created onwards
- A work of art (as a substitute here for “a message”) has the intentions of the creator and creation process within it, and carries those forwards whether it is observed by human eyes or not
- A human stumbling upon the art and understanding any part of its message is not the key that unlocks the potential of the work of art, proves its worth, or justifies its existence
- The work of art justifies its own existence by existing

- Thinking about “experimental” as a genre
- And how creations that don’t fit into our preexisting well defined categories are just kind of labelled “experimental” because people haven’t seen it before
- It’s not that it’s “wrong” per se, but it lends a sense of mediocrity and lack of mastery to the work.
- It insinuates by its name that there is no masterful work in this category; everything under this umbrella is just an experiment, made by someone who was simply testing something out, something strange and off and self contained
- Not to mention it (I suppose like every other label) is incredibly temporally situated; if the work becomes widespread, or if other works of art join its style, it suddenly gets a more prestigious title, or perhaps a newly created label, just for it
- “Experimental” is almost cute from the lens of “people are small and confused and don’t always know how to understand things”, but is crude from the lens of “people incessantly obfuscate works of art by thinking of them as the categories they fit into rather than what they are”, and this is nowhere more relevant than what is essentially the “miscellaneous” bucket that so many diverse and incredibly visionary works are thrown into

- Those same words being stored in a fundamentally non-human way - in buzzing and clicking, something we cannot understand innately - is to divorce them from the context in which they were created. They become orphaned and alone, a pocket of human experience suffocated under layers of technology and abstraction, so that no human being coming across the information in that state could ever know what is is

- Realizing recently that I don’t take breaks from “actual work”, i only take breaks from breaks

- I take a break from the break
- And from the next one
- An always ascending staircase of breaks from one another
- It’s not a thing of recognizing when you need a break and when you don’t; it’s recognizing when you need a break from the break you’re on. Going back to the same activity isn’t leaving your break backwards, it’s leaving it forwards

- This is most certainly not a new realization, but I’m not sure if I’ve explicitly codified it in my entries, and the previous entry made me think of it
- Art/work/progress that you end up throwing away is not wasted!
- If you spend 2 hours or a whole day or even a week fitfully scribbling and throwing things away and trashing ideas and shitting out terrible awful garbage ideas, that is NOT wasted time
- I am a firm firm believer that no time spent going down wrong pathways is wasted time
- (entirely separate conversation is “what do I consider to be wasted time” which I just typed out 2 paragraphs for and then deleted it all, which tells me that is DEFINITELY a conversation for another day or another entry)
- Your mind has to work through those incorrect pathways before it can find the right one
- Learning is fundamentally a process of going down wrong pathways until you a) understand that they’re wrong and b) understand WHY they’re wrong, before you can find the paths that actually do work for you
- But you need to see all those wrong pathways before you can see which ones are “right”!
- If you are ever going to make progress by yourself in art like this and genuinely build your own skill, you NEED to have sessions of fruitless and “unproductive” progress
- Because newflash, you can still make a fuck ton of progress in 4 hours even if you ultimately have thrown away every idea you’ve tried and are started with another blank canvas at the end of it
- Because think of all those bad ideas that you had to sift through! There is no magical future where you DIDN’T have to sift through those bad ideas, because you didn’t know they were bad until you tried them!!
- “Progress” is not only what ends up staying in the final version; “progress” does not have to be seen or heard to exist. Simply sifting through bad ideas and working out mental muscles are all progress, even if none of those things are “on the canvas” when you finally do make the work
- Can also be thought of as; sketches and early concept art are progress toward the finished rendered art piece. You can’t see them in the finished art piece, but certainly nobody will say that they were not meaningful progress that led there
- On that same vein, very early sketches of crude representations may only survive for a short while before the first “usable” sketch is produced, but those crude sketches are nevertheless an important part on the journey to making the “actual/useful” sketch, which in turn was an important point of progress towards the final piece
- And, even further back on the same vein, the 4 or 5 other ideas that you had tried (each of which with their own process of sketching → concept → rendering, and each of which getting cut short somewhere along the road because you didn’t like them) were ALSO all important towards the final piece
- Even though those ideas are not even the same idea or concept as the actual art piece you end up finishing, it was nevertheless important for you to “get them out of your system” so that you COULD finally arrive on the idea you were actually gonna use!
- Enough of the self hate of “i didn’t make any progress gahhh I’m no closer” - literally everything you’ve done has gotten you closer to what you want to do, you just don’t know it yet because YOU can’t see the path yet, but that doesn’t mean that you aren’t on the path
- Genuine progress sometimes looks like dead ends and back tracking and failed/truly “garbage” idea
- Progress includes genuine garbage
- Another way of phrasing the same idea:
- it’s easy to see yourself as “losing progress” if you get hours into a piece only to realize you don’t like it and starting over with a blank canvas
- In terms of what’s in front of you, it looks like you regressed because you are “back at the starting point” - i.e. you were at 0% when you first started 3 hours ago, and now you’re back at 0%
- but the progress bar does not include only the time spent on the “final version”, it includes everything
- At that 3 hour mark where you’re looking at a blank canvas, you are actually 25% of the way there.
- It may not SEEM like it, but what you don’t realize is that on the way to 100% (finally completed, to a degree that you’re proud of, the finishing touches of the full final piece) a completely blank canvas appears at 25%, 32%, and 47%, AND 64%.
- In YET ANOTHER WAY of phrasing the same idea:
- Imagine watching back a video from when you first sat down to work to when you finished the final piece you ended up making
- Just because the first half of the video is you working on things that never actually make it into the final piece, that half is nevertheless still part of the video
- it’s not like you only started working halfway through - no, you were working the entire time!

- However, public-facing news sources and articles do not paint the same story
- They all but completely say (and in some cases, they do flatly say) that “the ending had already been planned and recorded before the mangaka’s death, don’t worry. - But why?
- The news outlet reporting the story has no stake in whether or not Berserk’s continuation does well or not. They are not affiliated with the series at all. The continuation could tank and they would not be affected

- You will “fall in and out of love” so many times
- Embrace it
- Not engaging with something does not mean it is not a part of you, that it no longer means anything to you

- things are not important to you only when they take up your time

- And this all sits within larger and more overarching oscillations of periods of months or years where I will make more art for a track of a few years and not make as much for a track of a few years
- I will still have breaks during the period of the large oscillation where I make a lot of art, and I will still make art sometimes during the period of the large oscillation where I don’t make as much art
- Oscillations stacks, and it’s not a matter of trying to control the oscillations or even predict them, it’s simply a matter of learning to trust the oscillations
- Once you trust in the oscillations, you will be able to actually let go of your drive to make art during the period of time that you aren’t driven to make art without feeling guilty, and because of that, you will be able to experience *whatever else you are doing* during that time frame more fully
- Which, in turn, will enhance the experience of when the oscillations DO put you in a period where you’re making art again
- Breaks from things are important to actually enhance your relationships with the things when you ARE engaged in them
- Allow yourself to not do things without forcing yourself to; if you don’t want to, you don’t want to, and it’s really that simple; if it is important to you, you will naturally come back to it one day, I promise. - I was hiking on a trail the other day, and on nature trails I really enjoy finding spots along the way to sit and admire the trees and think for a little bit. Out in the forest in a really great place to do that
- Historically, I have walked a minute or two off the path to do this so that I am not “in anyone’s way” when I do this, just out of the latent knowledge that it would be “weird” if I did.
- However, this time I couldn’t be bothered, and plus there was such a nice spot to sit right on the edge of the trail, so I sit down for a little while
- Someone comes up behind me - usually, if I spot them before they see me, I get up and start walking out of a social anxiety to make it seem to them that I was always just walking
- But this time they saw me first and it would have been really obvious that I started walking because of them, so I committed to the bit and stayed where I was
- They passed me, and sure enough, they called out “you okay?”
- I assured them I was already, and they followed up with a question to make sure that I was indeed “just chilling” and didn’t need any help or anything
- On the surface, kind of them to check up on me
- But also, the only thing they picked up on that caused them to jump to the conclusion that I may not be okay was that I was sitting still, and doing nothing
- Had I been on my phone, or writing, I feel confident that they may not have said anything to me. But the fact that I was sitting and doing nothing stood out to them
- That same day, I was in my room and someone came in to talk to me, and at the time I had just come back from that very hike so I was just kinda sitting on my bed resting and thinking.
- They didn’t mention anything, but it was simply clear from their face and behavior when they first entered the room that they thought it was strange that I was simply doing nothing
- All this anecdotal evidence is simply to back up the point that people find it strange to see people do nothing
- Especially in “today’s times”, people in society or in public are so driven to be doing something. It becomes a compulsion for a lot of people to “do something” with their time, because otherwise “they are wasting it”
- In fact, as far as I can tell, the most/only socially acceptable form of doing nothing is to see people outside laying down in the grass or something, and that’s because they ARE viewed as doing something with their time - they are resting! They are filling their time with resting
- But to see someone not obviously doing something but also not obviously resting - i.e. simply sitting somewhere, upright, doing nothing else - has become a strange sight for many people
- I don’t really care about looking strange, what I care about is the fact that this stems from how so few people regularly make any time in their day to do nothing
- It has become a rarity, a special occurrence, just to see someone sitting and thinking!
- That shit is necessary! People need that time! As far as I’m concerned, everybody should make sure that there is some time in their day where they are sitting and doing nothing except letting their mind exercise itself out by going through whatever thoughts it has to go through, or even better yet, simply sitting and not even thinking
